title: Federal Judge Dismisses Trump Administration's Antisemitism Lawsuit Against Harvard
excerpt: U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns ruled that the government's allegations of campus antisemitism were 'too isolated and episodic' to establish ongoing civil rights violations at the university.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit alleging Harvard failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from discrimination
  • The judge found the government's evidence was 'too isolated and episodic' to prove ongoing violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
  • The lawsuit sought to halt $2.6 billion in federal grants and require Harvard to repay millions in prior funding
  • The Justice Department said it disagrees with the ruling and is assessing next steps

Judge Rules Evidence Too 'Isolated and Episodic'

A federal judge in Boston on Thursday dismissed the Trump administration's multi-billion-dollar lawsuit against Harvard University, ruling that the government failed to plausibly show an ongoing pattern of antisemitic discrimination on campus.

https://x.com/RedWavePress/status/2087977972858810369

U.S. District Judge Richard G. Stearns, a Clinton appointee, wrote that the incidents cited by the administration were "too isolated and episodic" to establish that Harvard was in systematic violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which bans discrimination based on race, color, and national origin in programs receiving federal funding, according to Reuters.

The government's complaint, filed on March 20, had alleged that Harvard "turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis" and was "deliberately indifferent" to harassment of Jewish students, according to USA Today.

What the Lawsuit Claimed

The Trump administration pointed to a series of incidents following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. The complaint described instances in which Jewish students were "spit on in the face for wearing a yarmulke, stalked on campus, and jeered by peers with calls of 'Heil Hitler,'" according to CNN.

The lawsuit alleged that students were deliberately excluded from Gaza war protests, that antisemitic messages were posted on a campus app, and that Harvard administrators failed to act properly on Jewish students' complaints.

In financial terms, the administration sought to halt $2.6 billion in existing federal grants and asked the court to require Harvard to repay millions in grant payments made during the alleged period of noncompliance, CNN reported.

Judge Finds Claims Outdated

Stearns found that the government's allegations were "almost entirely" limited to the 2023-2024 school year, with only three additional incidents cited from March 2025, according to USA Today. The judge clarified that his decision was "limited to the specific circumstances" of the case.

"The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division is actively investigating antisemitism nationwide. The Civil Rights Division has an extensive and active portfolio of antisemitism enforcement."

— Harmeet Dhillon, DOJ Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights

Harmeet Dhillon, the Justice Department's assistant attorney general for civil rights, said the administration disagrees with the ruling and is assessing next steps, according to CNN.

Harvard's First Amendment Defense

The dismissal is the latest chapter in a protracted battle between the Ivy League university and the White House, which has featured multiple lawsuits and intermittent negotiations. Harvard has argued that the government's pressure campaign — including threats to withhold funding — represents an unconstitutional overstep.

"This litigation is a continuation of the Government's ongoing campaign of retaliation against Harvard for refusing to capitulate to government demands and for exercising its First Amendment rights," Harvard attorneys wrote in court filings, according to CNN.

Harvard acknowledged in its filings that it had previously fallen short in addressing antisemitism, but pointed to what it called "sustained, institution-wide efforts" since October 2023 to address the issue, documented in a 300-page report by the university's Presidential Task Force on Combating Antisemitism and Anti-Israeli Bias.

Broader Context for Higher Education

While Trump's pressure campaign has yielded policy changes at other American universities, Harvard has largely refused to comply with sweeping government demands, according to CNN. The case is one of several confrontations between the administration and elite educational institutions over federal funding and campus policies.

The ruling comes at a sensitive time for universities across the country navigating campus protests, federal funding disputes, and questions about the line between political speech and harassment. For Indian-American students and faculty at elite institutions — who make up a significant share of Harvard's graduate and research programs — the outcome underscores the continuing uncertainty around campus climate, federal oversight, and the future of government funding to higher education.
